strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies genuine limitations in existing benchmarks—single-object focus, game-world scenarios overlooked, and text-only evaluation inadequacy. Compelling examples (Figure 2) justify the dual-reference approach.

Comprehensive scope and taxonomy: 8 primary dimensions × 18 sub-dimensions covering both real-world and game-world scenarios represent a significant expansion beyond prior work (RISE, KRIS), with thoughtful hierarchical organization.

Methodologically sound dual-reference evaluation: Combines textual and ground-truth image references—a sensible contribution. Clear formulation of Instruction Following, Visual Consistency, and Visual Quality with transparent weighting.

Well-engineered multi-scenario data synthesis: Scenario-specific strategies (VLM-scaled prompts for real-world, programmatic generation for game-world) are thoughtful. Multi-stage filtering pipeline (deduplication, VLM-based quality, human inspection by 8 annotators) demonstrates genuine quality control.

Extensive experimental validation: 15+ models benchmarked; comprehensive evaluation across UniREditBench, RISEBench, and KRISBench. Strong qualitative results (Figures 6–10) convincingly demonstrate model behaviors and UniREdit-Bagel superiority (especially +17.08 on game scenarios).
High data quality emphasis: Detailed documentation of filtering stages, human review process with web interfaces, and deduplication strategies enhance reproducibility and reliability.
Clear presentation: Well-organized structure with effective visualizations (Figures 1, 3, 4) and comprehensive supplementary material.
weaknesses: Single VLM evaluator creates bias and limits validation: Only GPT-4.1 used as judge with no comparison to Claude, Gemini, or open-source alternatives. Introduces potential circularity when evaluating GPT-4o baseline and raises concerns about evaluator consistency.

Missing inter-annotator agreement (IAA) metrics: No Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's α, or other IAA statistics reported for human annotations. Critical for assessing ground truth reliability and reproducibility.
Arbitrary evaluation weighting scheme without ablation: α₁=0.5, α₂=0.3, α₃=0.2 lack justification. No sensitivity analysis or comparison to alternative aggregation methods.

Lack of statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance testing, or effect size reporting. Benchmark size (2,700) and per-category sample size (150) not justified. Claims of improvement may lack statistical significance.

Synthetic data concerns and circular dependency: UniREdit-Data-100K entirely synthetic (VLM-generated text/CoT, synthetic images). Similar VLM/generative methods used for both dataset creation and benchmark construction, even if different samples—raises distribution leakage concerns.

Incomplete evaluation of dual-reference approach: No ablation directly comparing dual-reference vs. text-only evaluation on same samples. No human evaluation validating whether dual-reference correlates better with human judgments.

Game-world scenario limitations: Only 8 game types—limited diversity and representativeness. Python-generated images lack visual realism compared to actual game screenshots. No validation against human-annotated or real games.

No human performance baseline or error analysis: Missing upper-bound performance. No systematic analysis of which reasoning types models consistently fail on, limiting insights into benchmark utility.
Minimal modeling novelty: UniREdit-Bagel is standard fine-tuning (Bagel + CoT loss + image loss). Primary contribution is dataset-driven; architectural/algorithmic innovations absent.
Reproducibility gaps: Code/data release status unclear. VLM prompts for evaluation underspecified. Computational costs (annotation hours, evaluation expense) not discussed.

strengths: Well-motivated benchmark addressing genuine gaps: expands beyond single-object edits to multi-object interactions and provides dual-reference (text + image) evaluation, substantiating claims with clear examples (e.g., Figure 2).

Comprehensive taxonomy with 8 primary dimensions and 18 sub-categories, organized systematically across real-world and game-world scenarios, significantly broader than prior work (SmartEdit, RISE, KRIS).

Thoughtful multi-scenario data synthesis pipeline with distinct strategies for real-world (text→image scaling) and game-world (programmatic generation) that incorporates automated filtering and human inspection.
Strong empirical validation: UniREdit-Bagel achieves best overall performance (78.87) and demonstrates out-of-distribution improvements on RISEBench, validating dataset quality.
Large-scale training resource: UniREdit-Data-100K (100K+ samples) with chain-of-thought annotations enables reproducible model fine-tuning validation.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: dual-reference evaluation is straightforward (VLM compares output vs. text + image), data synthesis uses existing techniques (VLM scaling, diffusion models, standard filtering), and model training is standard supervised fine-tuning with CoT supervision. No novel methodologies are introduced.

Critical evaluation methodology flaws: (1) No human evaluation—benchmark validated entirely via GPT-4.1 without human studies to verify alignment; (2) Scoring weights (α₁=0.5, α₂=0.3, α₃=0.2) unjustified with no ablation; (3) Single evaluator introduces systematic bias; (4) No inter-rater reliability or confidence intervals; (5) No statistical significance testing.

Dataset validation concerns: Inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ) not reported for 8 human annotators; filtering pipeline opaque (no quantification of rejection rates at each stage); VLM-based prompt scaling introduces systematic vocabulary/phrasing biases that propagate through dataset.

Questionable scope: Game-world scenarios (Sudoku, Tic-Tac-Toe, Word Search) are visual reasoning tasks, not image editing. ~50% of benchmark (4/8 primary dimensions) allocated to games dilutes focus on actual image editing and creates unfair comparisons for models trained on real edits.

Insufficient analysis: No failure mode analysis or investigation of why models succeed/fail on specific dimensions; missing correlation analysis between dimensions; absent bias analysis regarding object/scenario representation; minimal investigation into what the benchmark reveals about model capabilities.

Reproducibility severely compromised: No code/data availability announced (only 'project page' referenced); critical hyperparameters unspecified (λ_text and λ_img for loss weighting); hand-crafted seed prompts not provided; inference details vague ('official settings'). Replication would be difficult.

Weak out-of-distribution generalization: UniREdit-Bagel achieves only 18.3% on RISEBench, still far below GPT-4o (28.9%) and comparable to Nano Banana (32.8%), undermining claims of strong reasoning-based generalization.

Missing critical experiments: No human evaluation of benchmark samples or scoring; no ablation on evaluation weights; no CoT supervision ablation; no comparison of VLM-generated vs. human-written instructions; no training variance across multiple runs.

strengths: Addresses a significant gap in existing image editing benchmarks by extending coverage from single-object attribute changes to multi-object interactions and game-world scenarios with human-defined rules, filling a clear need in the field

Introduces a principled dual-reference evaluation methodology combining textual and ground-truth image references, with compelling motivation (Figure 2) showing how text-only evaluation can lead to inflated scores

Comprehensive and well-organized benchmark design with hierarchical structure (8 primary × 18 sub-dimensions, ~150 samples per category), spanning diverse reasoning types across both real-world and game-world contexts

Sophisticated multi-scenario data synthesis pipeline with distinct strategies tailored to real-world (VLM-based text scaling) and game-world (Python programmatic) scenarios, including rigorous multi-stage filtering with deduplication, VLM quality assessment, and human inspection

Extensive experimental validation across 10+ baseline models (closed and open-source) with comprehensive benchmarking on multiple datasets (UniREditBench, RISEBench, KRISBench), revealing clear model-specific strengths and weaknesses

Large-scale training resource (UniREdit-Data-100K with 100K+ samples) with high-quality chain-of-thought annotations that demonstrably improve model performance, with UniREdit-Bagel achieving strong results (78.87 vs. 71.64 for GPT-4o)
Clear experimental presentation with both quantitative results and qualitative visualizations; detailed appendix with filtering procedures and annotation interfaces supports reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—the benchmark is primarily a data contribution; individual components (VLM-based evaluation, synthetic data generation) apply existing techniques without fundamental advances; dual-reference evaluation is a reasonable incremental improvement but not groundbreaking

Evaluation relies entirely on GPT-4.1 as sole evaluator without inter-rater reliability studies with human annotators; no analysis of potential systematic biases introduced by VLM evaluation, weakening confidence in assessment reliability

Evaluation metric weights (0.5/0.3/0.2 for instruction following/consistency/quality) appear arbitrary with no ablation study or justification provided; ground-truth image availability during evaluation could bias toward literal matching rather than true semantic understanding

Data quality concerns: heavy reliance on Gemini-2.5-Pro for scaling real-world data introduces potential systematic biases; human annotation details sparse with inter-annotator agreement not reported; game-world data from Python programs lacks visual diversity and realism despite logical correctness

Insufficient depth of analysis: missing error analysis on specific failure modes, no investigation of which reasoning dimensions are hardest, no ablation studies on evaluation components, no human performance baselines for reference

Evidence of overfitting to benchmark: UniREdit-Bagel shows large gains on UniREditBench (+7.23 over GPT-4o) but much smaller gains on out-of-distribution RISEBench (18.3% vs. 28.9% for GPT-4o), suggesting the model may overspecialize to the benchmark distribution

Reproducibility gaps: dataset availability only claimed (not confirmed), some filtering thresholds (e.g., 0.7 semantic similarity) lack justification, pre-trained VAE model specification missing, no code release mentioned

Game-world scenario design choices not thoroughly justified—these comprise ~50% of benchmark but practical relevance to real editing tasks unclear; Python programmatic generation ensures logic but compromises visual realism; limited discussion of whether game reasoning transfers to real-world editing

Statistical rigor lacking: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or inter-rater agreement metrics; sample size per category (~150) is relatively small; no analysis of category-specific performance distributions or data balance in training

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Clearly articulates gaps in existing benchmarks (single-object focus, neglect of multi-object interactions, game-world reasoning, reliance on text-only evaluation)
Novel dual-reference evaluation protocol: Thoughtfully combines textual and visual references with multi-dimensional VLM-based scoring, addressing genuine limitations of text-only evaluation

Comprehensive and systematic benchmark design: 2,700 curated samples across 8 primary dimensions and 18 sub-dimensions covering both real-world and game-world scenarios with 150 human-inspected examples per category

Scalable data synthesis pipeline: Well-designed multi-scenario approach with separate strategies for real-world (VLM-based CoT expansion) and game-world (Python-based logical generation) data generation, producing 100K+ high-quality CoT-annotated samples

Thorough experimental evaluation: Comprehensive benchmarking of 15+ models (closed and open-source), in-domain and out-of-distribution analysis, ablation studies, and human evaluation validating VLM-expert alignment
Clear presentation and writing: Well-organized paper with effective visualizations, comprehensive appendices, and qualitative examples demonstrating both model successes and failures
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: UniREdit-Bagel is a straightforward fine-tuning of Bagel with CoT supervision; no novel architectural or theoretical contributions

VLM-based evaluation limitations: Reliance on GPT-4.1 introduces potential biases and hallucinations; evaluation not ground-truth based but depends on human-curated references; circular reasoning concern using VLM to evaluate VLM outputs

Data quality and filtering concerns: Inter-annotator agreement not reported despite 8 annotators; semantic deduplication threshold (0.7) not validated; filtering pipeline details in appendix lack justification for fixed thresholds

Insufficient dataset analysis: Missing fine-grained error breakdown by dimension; limited CoT quality analysis (Table 10 shows only one example); no statistical analysis of sample difficulty distribution or potential imbalances

Game-world scenarios may be limited in scope: Only 8 game types included; while diverse, relatively constrained compared to real-world complexity; transferability to real-world reasoning unclear (Table 9 shows minimal gains)

Reproducibility concerns: No explicit discussion of dataset release timeline, licensing, or access procedures; data synthesis code availability unclear; some implementation details sparse (exact VLM prompts, inference configurations)

Limited error analysis and insights: Section 5.4 provides high-level discussion but lacks systematic breakdown of failure patterns; large performance gap between closed-source (81.8%) and open-source (56.9%) models not thoroughly investigated

Evaluation metric validation: Three scoring dimensions are intuitive but not independently validated; no user study confirming correlation with practical usefulness; weight selection based on GPT-4.1 correlation, not real applications

Lack of inter-rater reliability reporting: While human evaluation study (Table 4) shows correlation between VLM and expert scores, inter-annotator agreement metrics (κ, α) for the 8 expert annotators performing data curation not provided
Missing ethical discussion: Societal impact statement (Appendix M) is brief and generic; no discussion of potential misuse (e.g., generating misleading edited images)

strengths: Addresses genuine limitations of existing benchmarks by identifying two key challenges: narrow coverage of multi-object interactions and game-world scenarios, plus over-reliance on textual-only evaluation
Introduces dual-reference evaluation protocol incorporating both textual and ground-truth image references, a methodological improvement that enables more reliable assessment
Substantial scale with 2,700 carefully curated samples plus 100K synthetic samples, with systematic multi-stage filtering pipeline (deduplication, quality filtering, human inspection)
Comprehensive benchmarking of 15+ models with detailed quantitative and qualitative analysis, providing useful characterization of existing model capabilities
Well-organized hierarchical dimension framework (8 primary × 18 sub-dimensions) systematically covering diverse reasoning-based editing scenarios
Extensive supplementary material documenting data synthesis pipelines, game-world rules, and filtering strategies supports methodological transparency
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily data collection effort with minimal algorithmic contributions; UniREdit-Bagel is standard fine-tuning with no novel training strategies or architectures
Critical reproducibility gap: no mention of data or code release despite being a benchmark paper, making the resource inaccessible to the community and undermining its purpose

Problematic evaluation metric design: weight selection (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) lacks principled justification; single VLM (GPT-4.1) introduces vendor bias; substantial MAE between human and VLM scores (0.47-0.67) and only moderate correlation (r≈0.67) indicate the metric remains unreliable
Weak human evaluation baseline: only 6 annotators on 200 samples (3.3% of benchmark), no inter-annotator agreement reported, and insufficient expertise documentation
Insufficient analytical depth: benchmarking documents performance gaps but provides minimal insight into why models fail, what specific reasoning capabilities are lacking, or how to improve them

Weak justification for game-world scenarios: connection between puzzle-solving/maze navigation and real image editing capability is theoretical unestablished and empirically undemonstrated; ablation (Section G) shows mixed transferability results

Limited data synthesis analysis: no discussion of biases in VLM-generated real-world data, potential artifacts from Python code generation for game scenarios, or what filtering removes; CoT annotation quality not validated independently

Unclear generalization: most models score <20%, but unclear if this reflects unfair evaluation, inherent task difficulty, or genuine capability gaps; no in-distribution vs. out-of-distribution analysis; Table 3 shows extreme performance variance across scenarios without disambiguation
Game-world data transfer questionable: Table 9 shows game-world data sometimes hurts real-world performance, contradicting a primary motivation for their inclusion

Missing ablations and analyses: no ablation on CoT annotation impact, sensitivity to VLM choice, inter-scenario correlation analysis, or systematic error categorization; limited investigation into what each filtering stage removes

strengths: Addresses a critical gap in image editing benchmarks by focusing on reasoning-based tasks that require multi-object interactions and complex contextual understanding, which existing benchmarks overlook

Introduces a novel dual-reference evaluation protocol combining textual and ground-truth image references, with user study validation showing strong alignment with human judgment (MAE values in Fig. 7)
Comprehensive benchmark design spanning 8 primary reasoning dimensions and 18 sub-categories, covering both realistic and game-world scenarios systematically organized in a hierarchical taxonomy

Rigorous multi-stage data curation pipeline with instruction deduplication (exact and semantic similarity), automated quality filtering across 6 dimensions, and human inspection using dedicated web interfaces
Large-scale dataset (100K samples) with high-quality chain-of-thought reasoning annotations enabling future model development and training
Systematic benchmarking of 14 models (8 closed-source, 6 open-source) revealing clear performance patterns and identifying game-world scenarios as particularly challenging for current models
UniREdit-Bagel demonstrates meaningful improvements over existing models (7.8% gain in game scenarios), validating the dataset utility while surpassing certain closed-source baselines
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and transparent methodology, including explicit mathematical formulation of the evaluation metric and justified design choices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in the model component: UniREdit-Bagel is primarily a fine-tuned version of existing Bagel architecture using standard losses, making the model contribution incremental

VLM-based evaluation relies on GPT-4.1 as sole judge without exploring potential evaluator bias or cross-validating with alternative VLMs; user study for validation is relatively modest (200 samples, 6 experts)

Game-world scenario data is synthetically generated via Python programs and LLM conversion rather than collected naturally, potentially missing complexities of real interactive reasoning; no human validation of scenario coherence
Insufficient systematic analysis of failure modes: while Section K shows examples, there is no categorization or clustering of failure types beyond anecdotal visual cases

Weight selection for the evaluation metric (ω₁=0.5, ω₂=0.3, ω₃=0.2) justified only through correlation analysis in Appendix B; no sensitivity analysis showing robustness to weight changes, and achieved correlation is modest (r≈0.83-0.84)
No computational cost analysis for data synthesis pipeline or training time discussion; scalability and practical applicability of the dual-reference evaluation not addressed
Potential benchmark saturation risk as models continue improving; limited forward-looking discussion about robustness to future model capabilities beyond GPT-4.1
Limited exploration of transferability: game-world to real-world improvement shown (Table 9) but reverse direction and broader cross-domain effects not analyzed
